turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Come on back, I'll get a blood pressure before she sees you. Just rest that arm on the desk, palm up.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure thing. I actually brought the little notebook where I write the home numbers, my sister bought it for me, she says if it's not written down it didn't happen, which is dramatic but, you know, she's not wrong.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sitting blood pressure is 148 over 92, heart rate 78. I'll drop those in the chart.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): 148 over 92, yeah. Mornings at the kitchen table I've been landing in the one-fifties over the low nineties, especially if I measure before coffee.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Doctor's just finishing something on the computer. She'll be in.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this screen is still thinking. What brings you in?

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this cough, a dry one, nothing comes up. It's been going on for weeks, and I keep connecting it to a cold I had, the kind that starts as sniffles and then turns into a tickle. About four weeks, maybe a little longer, and I can't pin the exact day. It was the tail end of that cold, or right after I thought I was over it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hold on, it blinked. Say how long again?

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): About four weeks, maybe a little more. It's a dry tickle, worse at night when I lie down, maybe every few minutes while I'm trying to sleep, and it eases if I sit up. Warm tea helps a bit, and talking on the phones at work sets it off. In the daytime it's more off and on, not constant.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever with it now?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever now. Back at the start of the cold I ran a little temperature, but that was gone before this cough really settled in and stayed.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any phlegm, shortness of breath, chest pain?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No phlegm, no shortness of breath, no chest pain. I still walk the dog around the block, no problem, I just sound annoying.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Give me a second, I opened the wrong med list. Are you on ramipril?

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, ramipril, five milligrams, by mouth, every morning, for the blood pressure. I started it about three weeks ago, or it might be four, right around that cold. I haven't missed one. I park the bottle by the coffee maker so it's automatic.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Three weeks or four, the row jumped. What was the dose, one more time?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Five milligrams. Once every morning.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): And just so nobody mixes the bottles up, my sister takes lisinopril, ten milligrams, that's printed right on her bottle. She had a cough last winter and she was convinced it was her pill, and her doctor told her it was only a cold. Hers, not mine. I don't take lisinopril.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, her lisinopril stays hers. You mentioned an old test was borderline?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Last year, before they started any blood pressure pill, they did bloodwork and said the creatinine was borderline. They didn't give me a number I can remember, just the word borderline, we'll watch it. Same draw, they said the cholesterol was fine.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Borderline creatinine, no figure. Swelling in the ankles?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. I don't smoke, never have. I'll have a glass of wine some weekends, not even every weekend, more like if we're at my sister's.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medications?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing I know of. Penicillin was fine back when I had that tooth infection, years ago, no rash or anything.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the high blood pressure, how long has that been the diagnosis?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): About two years. I tried less salt and more walking for a while, which helped a little and then it crept back up, so the other clinic put me on the ramipril.

[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay, thinking out loud while this reloads. A dry cough can linger for weeks after a cold, that's one way this goes. Ramipril is an ACE inhibitor and those can cause a dry cough, that's another way. I am not going to conclude which this is, and I am not calling it an ACE-inhibitor cough.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're saying it could still just be the cold hanging on? Because that's what I've been telling my husband every night, that it's the cold, not the new pill.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): It could be the cold, and it could be the ramipril. I won't pick one. What I am going to do is stop the ramipril and switch you to losartan, fifty milligrams, once a day.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Losartan, fifty. If it was the pill, would the cough stop by the weekend? I was on some forum reading horror stories, actually no, forget the forum, it was people arguing, not useful.

[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Please don't time it and decide. If ramipril is part of it, the cough can take weeks to fade, and a cough after a cold can do the exact same thing. I'm still not putting a name on the cause.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I use up the ramipril I've got, or is today the last day? I already swallowed this morning's with breakfast.

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stop the ramipril today. Nothing more after this morning's dose. Start the losartan tomorrow morning, by mouth, fifty milligrams, once daily, food or no food, either is fine.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I stand up and get woozy at work? I'm on the phones, I can't really lie down in the cubicle, there's barely room.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you feel lightheaded, sit down and call the office. If you miss a dose of the losartan, skip it, don't double the next one.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): What about that kidney thing they called borderline? I've been wondering if somebody should look again, I even circled it in the notebook.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not ordering a chest x-ray today. If the cough hasn't settled in three weeks, then we can consider a chest x-ray. I do want a basic metabolic panel at the follow-up visit, that's the plan, so we can recheck that kidney number.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): So I come back in three weeks? I can do mornings, before I go in to work, that's easier than lunch.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, follow up in three weeks. Come sooner if you get a fever, if you start coughing up colored mucus, or if you can't catch your breath.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): And the tea, I can keep doing that? It's just grocery-store black tea, nothing fancy, sometimes with honey if we have it.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tea is fine. I'm going to have the front desk send the losartan over and put you on the schedule. This login just dumped me again, one second.
[SEG0042] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Three weeks, and losartan fifty milligrams to the pharmacy we have on file?
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Send it, and flag ramipril as stopped so they don't refill it.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the CVS on Maple. Could you spell losartan? I write the name, the dose, the date, all of it, otherwise I'll second-guess myself in the parking lot.
[SEG0045] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): L-O-S-A-R-T-A-N, fifty milligrams once a day. You're on the books for three weeks, we'll text a reminder, and ramipril is marked stopped.

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. The job is insurance claims, phones all day, so when I said talking sets the cough off, I mean hours of it, not a quick chat. Sorry, I know I already said the phone part.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): I heard you. I am still not assigning a cause to the cough. Anything else, or did we cover it?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I think that's everything. The home readings really have been in that same ballpark as the one she got today, not a surprise.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right. We'll see you in three weeks.
[SEG0050] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): The prescription is queued to the CVS on Maple, and the visit is on the schedule.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Just to say it back, tomorrow morning is the first losartan, and I do not take ramipril tonight even if the bottle is sitting there.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's right. Take care.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and the cold, the runny nose part of it, that cleared. I don't still have the sniffles, it's only the cough now.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): No current runny nose. I've got to get to the next chart.
[SEG0055] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): You're all set to go whenever. Watch for the text.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: All details supported except certainty=uncertain; symptom itself is clearly reported present.
bad.text: dry cough (category=respiratory, status=present, duration=approximately 4 weeks, maybe a little more, frequency=worse at night, about every few minutes while trying to sleep; off and on during the day, onset=tail end of a cold or just after, exact day unknown, temporality=current, aggravating_factors=lying down, talking on the phones at work, relieving_factors=sitting up, warm tea, reported_by=patient, certainty=uncertain)

bad.reason: Creatinine bloodwork was completed, but not requested_by patient; patient only reports prior testing.
Cholesterol was checked previously, but not requested_by patient in transcript.

omissions.text: Home blood pressure readings have been in the 150s over low 90s in the mornings, and are in the same ballpark as today's office reading.
Sitting blood pressure was recorded as sitting blood pressure 148/92, not just a blood pressure value without position.
Patient reports no problem walking the dog around the block despite the cough, supporting no exertional shortness of breath.

Past labs were described as 'borderline creatinine' and cholesterol fine last year before any blood pressure medicine; the recorded investigations incorrectly attribute these as requested_by=patient rather than being prior tests the patient reported.
The doctor explicitly stated uncertainty about the cough cause and did not diagnose ACE-inhibitor cough: it could be lingering post-cold or due to ramipril, and the doctor would not pick one cause.
Losartan should start tomorrow morning after stopping ramipril today, since today's ramipril dose was already taken.
Losartan instructions included that it may be taken with food or without food.
